L16: > Abstract:Long-running AI agents outlive initiating processes through credentials, delegated tasks, queues, callbacks, reservations, and provider-side operations. Cancellation, process exit, and credential revocation neither close every pre-cut carrier nor distinguish independently authorized shared work.
L17: We define root-scoped authorization quiescence: for each manifested sink, a certificate accounts for every cut-relevant acceptance under the retired root-epoch atom that precedes its local fence and excludes protected acceptance under that atom after the fence, while permitting exact rebind to a current, independently sufficient support.
L18: > The root-scoped quiescence protocol linearizes a root cut, fences old-root expansion and protected sinks, represents alternative and conjunctive authority as antichains of minimal sufficient root sets, and composes provider-frontier certificates into a cutset over registered old-root paths. Exact channel-token accounting reconciles transfers; missing or conflicting evidence remains indeterminate.
L19: Under stated assumptions, we prove post-cut issuer non-expansion, support-sound projection, compositional soundness under exact channel conservation, independent-support preservation, merge-order independence, and crash/replay stability.
L20: > A provider-free late-effect test suite matches 17/17 registered outcomes. Two cancellation-only and one cut-only execution accept the same class of already scheduled late effect; two cut-plus-fence executions, one restart, and one stale-process execution reject it. L4: # Zero Knowledge (About) Encryption: A Comparative Security Analysis of Three Cloud-based Password Managers
L5: 
L6: Matteo Scarlata, ETH Zurich; Giovanni Torrisi and Matilda Backendal, USI, Lugano; Kenneth G. Paterson, ETH Zurich
L7: Zero Knowledge Encryption is a term widely used by vendors of cloud-based password managers. Although it has no strict technical meaning, the term conveys the idea that the server, who stores encrypted password vaults on behalf of users, is unable to learn anything about the contents of those vaults. The security claims made by vendors imply that this should hold even if the server is fully malicious.
L8: This threat model is justified in practice by the high sensitivity of vault data, which makes password manager servers an attractive target for breaches (as evidenced by a history of attacks).
L9: We examine the extent to which security against a fully malicious server holds true for three leading vendors who make the Zero Knowledge Encryption claim: Bitwarden, LastPass and Dashlane. Collectively, they have more than 60 million users and 23% market share. We present 12 distinct attacks against Bitwarden, 7 against LastPass and 6 against Dashlane.
L10: The attacks range in severity, from integrity violations of targeted user vaults to the complete compromise of all the vaults associated with an organisation. The majority of the attacks allow recovery of passwords. We have disclosed our findings to the vendors and remediation is underway.
L11: Our attacks showcase the importance of considering the malicious server threat model for cloud-based password managers. Despite vendors' attempts to achieve security in this setting, we uncover several common design anti-patterns and cryptographic misconceptions that resulted in vulnerabilities. We discuss possible mitigations and also reflect more broadly on what can be learned from our analysis by developers of end-to-end encrypted systems.

L8: # Position: AI Agents Need Authenticated Delegation
L9: 
L10: Tobin South, Samuele Marro, Thomas Hardjono, Robert Mahari, Cedric Deslandes Whitney, Alan Chan, Alex Pentland
L11: 
L12: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267:82211-82231, 2025.
L13: #### Abstract
L14: The rapid deployment of autonomous AI agents creates urgent challenges in the areas of authorization, accountability, and access control in task delegation. This position paper argues that authenticated and auditable delegation of authority to AI agents is a critical component of mitigating practical risks and unlocking the value of agents.
L15: To support this argument, we examine how existing web authentication and authorization protocols, as well as natural language interfaces to common access control mechanisms, can be extended to enable secure authenticated delegation of authority to AI agents.
L16: By extending OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with agent-specific credentials and using transparent translation of natural language permissions into robust scoping rules across diverse interaction modalities, we outline how authenticated delegation can be achieved to enable clear chains of accountability while maintaining compatibility with established authentication and web infrastructure for immediate compatibility. This work contributes to ensuring that agentic AI systems perform only appropriate actions.
L17: It argues for prioritizing delegation infrastructure as a key component of AI agent governance and provides a roadmap for achieving this.

Title: Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions
Authors: Jinghan Xu, Longze Fan, Zeyuan Wang, Xinjin Li, Hankai Liu
Date: Mon Aug  3 05:16:02 2026

Tool-using large language model agents frequently replan, retry failed operations, delegate tasks, and resume after crashes. These behaviors can cause one user authorization to be requested and executed multiple times under freshly issued token identifiers, even when each individual token is single-use. We call this failure semantic replay: exceeding the execution budget of a token-independent authorization instance rather than merely reusing an old token identifier. We show that identifier-local token consumption cannot prevent fresh reissuance unless the issuer retains monotonic durable state over the authorized action, confirmation event, and remaining execution budget. We introduce CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that follows proposal- and authority-level defenses, binds an authenticated user confirmation to a canonical action, and enforces transactional Issue-Prepare-Commit transitions. Across LLM-agent replanning, retry, delegation, concurrency, confirmation-replay, and crash-recovery scenarios, identifier-local tokens permit fresh semantic reissuance, whereas CapLease and an equally stateful Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission and, with an idempotent sink, duplicate external effects. Our results identify durable authorization state, rather than token representation alone, as the systems requirement for replay-resistant agent execution.

Title: Progent: Programmable Privilege Control for LLM Agents
Authors: Tianneng Shi, Jingxuan He, Zhun Wang, Linyu Wu, Hongwei Li, Wenbo Guo, Dawn Song
Date: Wed Apr 16 01:58:40 2025

LLM agents are an emerging form of AI systems where large language models (LLMs) serve as the central component, utilizing a diverse set of tools to complete user-assigned tasks. Despite their great potential, LLM agents pose significant security risks. When interacting with the external world, they may encounter malicious commands from attackers, leading to the execution of dangerous actions. A promising way to address this is by enforcing the principle of least privilege: allowing only essential actions for task completion while blocking unnecessary ones. However, achieving this is challenging, as it requires covering diverse agent scenarios while preserving both security and utility. We introduce Progent, the first privilege control mechanism for LLM agents. At its core is a domain-specific language for flexibly expressing privilege control policies applied during agent execution. These policies provide fine-grained constraints over tool calls, deciding when tool calls are permissible and specifying fallbacks if they are not. This enables agent developers and users to craft suitable policies for their specific use cases and enforce them deterministically to guarantee security. Thanks to its modular design, integrating Progent does not alter agent internals and requires only minimal changes to agent implementation, enhancing its practicality and potential for widespread adoption. To automate policy writing, we leverage LLMs to generate policies based on user queries, which are then updated dynamically for improved security and utility. Our extensive evaluation shows that it enables strong security while preserving high utility across three distinct scenarios or benchmarks: AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentPoison. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth analysis, showcasing the effectiveness of its core components and the resilience of its automated policy generation against adaptive attacks.

L16: > Abstract:Agentic systems now act with user secrets for APIs, messaging platforms, and cloud services. Today's agent runtimes typically implement authorization by exposure: enabling action means placing a reusable secret, or a reusable artifact derived from it, inside the runtime, so a transient prompt-injection or tool-side compromise becomes durable account compromise.
L17: Existing defenses cover adjacent pieces such as secret storage, scoped delegation, sender-constrained tokens, and runtime monitoring, but none states the combined requirement: an untrusted autonomous requester should be able to cause a user-authorized secret-backed operation without gaining reusable authority over it. We formalize this as the Agent Secret Use (ASU) problem and identify seven security properties any solution must satisfy, spanning authorization integrity and secret confidentiality.
L18: We propose the Secret-Use Delegation Protocol (SUDP), in which a requester proposes a canonical operation, the user authorizes it with a fresh authenticator-backed grant, and a custodian redeems the grant to perform the bounded use; reusable authority never crosses the requester boundary. We specialize SUDP for LLM-driven agents, where it applies whenever a tool call would exercise user-enrolled authority-bearing material.
L19: Under standard cryptographic assumptions, SUDP satisfies six of the seven properties; the seventh, runtime-memory confidentiality, is closed by composition with a hardware-rooted runtime. A reference implementation, available at 【12†this https URL†github.com】, adds sub-millisecond protocol overhead per mediated call.

L9: # Title:Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions
L10: 
L11: Authors:【5†Jinghan Xu】, 【6†Longze Fan】, 【7†Zeyuan Wang】, 【8†Xinjin Li】, 【9†Hankai Liu】
L12: 
L13: View a PDF of the paper titled Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions, by Jinghan Xu and 4 other authors
L14: 
L15: 【10†View PDF】 【11†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:Tool-using large language model agents frequently replan, retry failed operations, delegate tasks, and resume after crashes. These behaviors can cause one user authorization to be requested and executed multiple times under freshly issued token identifiers, even when each individual token is single-use. We call this failure semantic replay: exceeding the execution budget of a token-independent authorization instance rather than merely reusing an old token identifier.
L17: We show that identifier-local token consumption cannot prevent fresh reissuance unless the issuer retains monotonic durable state over the authorized action, confirmation event, and remaining execution budget. We introduce CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that follows proposal- and authority-level defenses, binds an authenticated user confirmation to a canonical action, and enforces transactional Issue-Prepare-Commit transitions.
L18: Across LLM-agent replanning, retry, delegation, concurrency, confirmation-replay, and crash-recovery scenarios, identifier-local tokens permit fresh semantic reissuance, whereas CapLease and an equally stateful Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission and, with an idempotent sink, duplicate external effects. Our results identify durable authorization state, rather than token representation alone, as the systems requirement for replay-resistant agent execution.

L10: 
L11: Authors:【6†Nils Palumbo】, 【7†Sarthak Choudhary】, 【8†Jihye Choi】, 【9†Guy Amir】, 【10†Prasad Chalasani】, 【11†Isil Dillig】, 【12†Somesh Jha】

L16: > Abstract:As agentic computing systems grow increasingly popular, they raise serious security concerns due to their susceptibility to various attacks. While prior research efforts aim to mitigate these concerns, they are often too coarse-grained and offer no formal correctness guarantees. In this work, we present a novel approach to agentic security based on runtime monitoring.
L17: Our method allows the user to specify their intended policy in Datalog and enforces the specified policy at runtime by constructing event graphs. When an agent is about to execute an action such as a tool call, our approach determines whether the action would violate the policy in light of the current system state and the history of past events. The action is then blocked or permitted accordingly.
L18: We implemented our approach and evaluated it across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating its merits in real-world settings. We view this work as a step towards agentic systems that are provably safe and secure.

L9: # Title:Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control
L10: 
L11: Authors:【6†Tianneng Shi】, 【7†Jingxuan He】, 【8†Zhun Wang】, 【9†Hongwei Li】, 【10†Linyu Wu】, 【11†Wenbo Guo】, 【12†Dawn Song】
L12:

L14: 
L15: 【13†View PDF】 【14†HTML (experimental)】
L16: > Abstract:AI agents interact with external environments through tool calls, exposing them to attacks like indirect prompt injection that can trigger unauthorized actions. Securing these agents is challenging: they behave autonomously and probabilistically, security requirements evolve depending on the user's task and execution state, and there is an inherent tradeofff between security and utility.
L17: > In this work, we introduce Progent, a novel framework that secures AI agents via privilege control. Progent represents privilege as a security policy consisting of symbolic rules over tool names and arguments. These rules specify which tool calls are allowed for task completion and which unnecessary ones are blocked for security. Every tool call is checked against such a policy through a deterministic procedure, enforcing the principle of least privilege.
L18: To handle diverse user tasks and evolving execution contexts, an LLM automatically generates the initial policy from the user's task and updates it during execution as new information arrives. Each proposed update is determined by an SMT solver to be either a narrowing (applied automatically) or an expansion (requiring explicit approval), ensuring that the agent's effective action space can only shrink without approval (monotonic confinement).
L19: This deterministic update mechanism preserves utility and prevents silent privilege escalation, even when adversarial inputs are present.
L20: > Our evaluation on popular benchmarks (i.e., AgentDojo and ASB) shows that Progent significantly reduces attack success rates while maintaining high utility. We further validate Progent's practicality by showcasing its effectiveness in real-world agent frameworks such as LangChain and OpenAI Agents SDK.

L34@P0: 1. Introduction
L35@P0: Passwords stubbornly remain the most prevalent authentication method and are unlikely to be replaced in the
L36@P0: foreseeable future [2], [4], [19], [20]. The average number of
L37@P0: accounts that users need to maintain has increased to 80-168
L38@P0: [30], [45], [48]. This brings great burdens for users to manage (e.g., create/remember/type) passwords. In response,
L39@P0: users often adopt vulnerable behaviors such as choosing
L40@P0: popular passwords (e.g., 123456 and password) [60],
L41@P0: reusing passwords [47], and creating passwords containing
L42@P0: personally identifiable information (PII) [59], which makes
L43@P0: password vulnerable to damaging password guessing attacks
L44@P0: [39], [47], [60], [61]. Besides, there are usability issues,
L45@P0: e.g., typos often occur when typing passwords, especially
L46@P0: on mobile devices. In a nutshell, managing a large number
L47@P0: of passwords is a great challenge for common human users.
L48@P0: Password managers (PMs), tools for helping users manage
L49@P0: credentials, are promising to alleviate this issue. Benefiting
L50@P0: from the free of human memorization, users can generate
L51@P0: strong (e.g., long and containing various characters) and
L52@P0: unique passwords for each credential by PMs. Users can
L53@P0: store their credentials into PMs, and unlock the PMs to get
L54@P0: their passwords when they need. PMs help users avoid vulnerable behaviors, and reduce the cognitive burden caused
L55@P0: by memorizing multiple passwords, striking a balance between password security and usability [24]. Therefore, PMs
L56@P0: are highly recommended by standard bodies (e.g., NIST [3]
L57@P0: and NCSC [1]) and security experts [31], [41], [67].
L58@P0: The security of PMs, given their centralization of sensitive
L59@P0: user credentials, has become a serious concern for both
L60@P0: industry [51], [57] and academia [26], [27], [38], [46],
L61@P0: [55]. LastPass [6] experienced data breaches three times
L62@P0: within past three years [9], [56]. While LastPass asserts
L63@P0: that no passwords were compromised in 2022, this breach
L64@P0: has recently been found disastrous and linked to a theft of
L65@P0: $4.4 million in cryptocurrency [9]. Furthermore, potential
L66@P0: security concerns have been identified as deterrents for users
L67@P0: in adopting PMs [10], [40], [44], [49], [50]. Users not
L68@P0: only fear data breaches in PMs but also exhibit limited
L69@P0: trust in entrusting all their credentials to a third party [10],
L70@P0: [49]. To instill more trust, several PMs assert that they
L71@P0: are “zero-knowledge” regarding users’ password vaults [13],
L72@P0: [36]. This term implies that the PMs only store encrypted
L73@P0: password vaults without knowledge of the actual contents.
L74@P0: In general, users are required to create a master password
L75@P0: to authenticate and manage password vaults. We characterize
L76@P0: the interaction between the client and the PM’s server
L77@P0: as the Master-Password-Protected Password Management
L78@P0: (M3PM) protocol. We define M3PM as a cryptographic
L79@P0: protocol that authenticates the client and ensures the password vault remains oblivious to the server side. Secure
L80@P0: encryption of password vaults does not necessarily ensure
L81@P0: a secure M3PM protocol. An inappropriate combination
L82@P0: of authentication and encryption mechanisms can introduce
L83@P0: vulnerabilities (see Sec. 5.4), and M3PM protocols encompass broader security properties beyond encryption (see Sec.
L84@P0-1: 4.1). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study tosystematically identify and analyze the security of M3PM
L85@P1: protocols. We focus on three research questions (RQs):
L86@P1: • RQ1: What M3PM protocols have been adopted by
L87@P1: existing password managers?
L88@P1: • RQ2: What defines a secure M3PM protocol?
L89@P1: • RQ3: Are existing password managers using M3PM
L90@P1: protocols secure under our security definitions?
L91@P1: To address these three questions, we develop a systematic methodology to understand the status quo of M3PM
L92@P1: protocols. This involves collecting and refining information
L93@P1: about M3PM protocols from 43 major PMs sourced from
L94@P1: academia and industry. We summarize the security properties of M3PM protocols and formalize ideal functionalities
L95@P1: to describe what constitutes an ideally secure M3PM protocol within the universal composability (UC) framework
L96@P1: [21]. This enables a systematic analysis of the M3PM
L97@P1: protocols to identify security vulnerabilities. In summary,
L98@P1: our contributions include:
L99@P1: • A methodology for identifying M3PM protocols.
L100@P1: We introduce a systematic methodology for identifying M3PM protocols across 36 popular industrial PMs and seven representative academic PMs.
L101@P1: Information about these protocols is sourced from
L102@P1: three primary channels: documentation, data logs,
L103@P1: and application code. We use an iterative process
L104@P1: of collection and verification to accurately identify
L105@P1: information on M3PM protocols, cryptographic algorithms, and metadata encryption.
L106@P1: • Ideal functionalities of M3PM protocols. We formalize the security properties of M3PM protocols
L107@P1: and present an ideal functionality FM3PM within the
L108@P1: UC framework. During our analysis of the collected
L109@P1: M3PM protocols, we iteratively revise and extend
L110@P1: this functionality to distinguish between explicit
L111@P1: authentication FM3PM-EA and implicit authentication FM3PM-IA. Inspired by previous work on
L112@P1: password-related protocols [8], [22], [25], [29], [33],
L113@P1: we introduce a relaxed functionality FrM3PM to
L114@P1: address guessing attacks and present FadM3PM to
L115@P1: accommodate protocols with additional secrets.
L116@P1: • Security analysis for M3PM protocols. We categorize four types of offline master password guessing attacks, and find 38 of 43 PMs cannot resist at least one type of offline guessing attack.
L117@P1: We summarize the circumstances that each M3PM
L118@P1: protocol fails to resist offline guessing attacks and
L119@P1: conclude that the current design of M3PM protocols,
L120@P1: without additional secrets or devices, suffers from
L121@P1: the low entropy of master passwords and heavily
L122@P1: relies on the effectiveness of slow hash or memoryhard functions. Additionally, we find fully plaintext
L123@P1: communication in Delinea Web, and uncover an
L124@P1: oracle attack where a corrupted server can learn
L125@P1: the encryption key of Passbolt. Overall, we give
L126@P1: provable analysis of eight distinct M3PM protocols
L127@P1: and prove the M3PM protocols of 1Password and
L128@P1: Multipassword realize FadM3PM-EA.
L129@P1: Responsible disclosure and ethical considerations. Given
L130@P1: the potential risks of users leaking their passwords, we have
L131@P1: disclosed our findings to the two affected PM vendors:
L132@P1: Delinea Web and Passbolt. In particular, we contacted
L133@P1: Delinea Web regarding the vulnerability. They confirmed
L134@P1: the vulnerability we identified but do not consider a malicious server as part of their threat model. Additionally, we
L135@P1: engaged in an in-depth discussion with Passbolt regarding
L136@P1: the identified vulnerability and provided recommendations
L137@P1: to mitigate the risks (see details in Sec. 5.4).
L138@P1: 2. Preliminary
L139@P1: 2.1. Password Managers
L140@P1: Password managers (PMs) are tools that help users manage their accounts. The basic management function of PMs
L141@P1: is to memorize passwords so that users can effortlessly
L142@P1: delegate their password management responsibilities to the
L143@P1: PMs, retrieving passwords as needed. Modern PMs offer
L144@P1: the capability to generate random passwords, and users can
L145@P1: tailor password settings, including length and character composition. During the login process on respective websites,
L146@P1: the autofill feature in PMs automatically populates users’
L147@P1: credentials, alleviating the need for manual typing. This
L148@P1: enhanced convenience attributed to autofill is a major driver
L149@P1: behind the adoption of PMs [49]. Furthermore, PMs employ
L150@P1: tools like the password strength meter, such as Zxcvbn [63],
L151@P1: to assess and identify weak passwords. Additionally, PMs
L152@P1: utilize compromised credential checking services, such as
L153@P1: Have I Been Pwned [5], to identify and alert users about
L154@P1: any passwords that may have been compromised or leaked.
L155@P1: In this work, we focus on the basic management function, i.e., memorizing passwords. Depending on the way
L156@P1: of memorizing passwords, PMs can be categorized into
L157@P1: two types [42]: (1) Retrieval PMs (e.g., 1Password and
L158@P1: LastPass) store users’ credentials in digital memory, commonly referred to as password vaults. These credentials
L159@P1: are then retrieved as needed during the user authentication
L160@P1: process; (2) Generative PMs (e.g., LessPass and SPHINX
L161@P1: [53]) create users’ credentials on demand by inputting the
L162@P1: master password and additional information such as URLs
L163@P1: and usernames into deterministic functions, such as OPRF
L164@P1: [53] or hash functions [52]. The result is the creation of
L165@P1: distinct passwords for different user accounts. In essence,
L166@P1: retrieval PMs store encrypted user-chosen credentials, like
L167@P1: an encrypted database, whereas generative PMs generate
L168@P1: passwords on behalf of different accounts.
L169@P1: 2.2. Related Work
L170@P1: At ESORICS’12, Gasti and Rasmussen [27] investigated
L171@P1: the storage format of password vaults. They gave two security definitions for password vaults: (1) Indistinguishability
L172@P1: of databases game corresponding to passive attackers; (2)
L173@P1: Malleability of chosen database game corresponding to
L174@P1: active attackers. According to their analysis, unencrypted
L175@P1-2: metadata would leak users’ privacy and give attackers theadvantage of distinguishing users’ password vaults and tampering vaults without integrity checks. Their work is the first
L176@P2: rigorous analysis for PMs, but it analyzed the storage format
L177@P2: instead of the M3PM protocol, which neglects authentication
L178@P2: of retrieval password vaults and offline guessing attacks of
L179@P2: the master passwords. Furthermore, their work analyzed 13
L180@P2: PMs in industry, while we give a more systematic analysis
L181@P2: across 36 industrial PMs and seven academic PMs. In 2020,
L182@P2: Oesch and Ruoti [46] replicated Gasti and Rasmussen’s [27]
L183@P2: study, finding PMs have improved in protecting metadata
L184@P2: but still leave some plaintext vulnerable. Replicating their
L185@P2: analysis, we find that after three years, 30 out of 43 PMs
L186@P2: still leave plaintext metadata (see details in Sec. 5.2).
L187@P2: Zhao et al. [69] analyzed the storage of two cloudbased PMs and found that insecure storage methods (e.g.,
L188@P2: the insecure relationship between master passwords and
L189@P2: authenticators) can leave the password vaults vulnerable. In
L190@P2: the same year, Zhao and Yue [68] showed five browser-based
L191@P2: PMs would be cracked once the encrypted information is
L192@P2: stolen. These works pointed out the potential vulnerability
L193@P2: of offline guessing attacks on master passwords and gave us
L194@P2: insights to conduct a systematic and rigorous analysis.
L195@P2: Bojinov et al. [17] and Chatterjee et al. [23] highlighted
L196@P2: that encryption using the master password alone cannot
L197@P2: withstand offline guessing attacks in the event of a leakage
L198@P2: of the encrypted password vault. They proposed novel
L199@P2: schemes, called honey vaults, to resist offline guessing attacks on leaked vaults. Inspired by their work, we formalize
L200@P2: the process of offline guessing attacks and emphasize that
L201@P2: the adversary’s prior knowledge significantly influences the
L202@P2: ability to attack honey vaults (see details in Sec. 5.1).
L203@P2: At CRYPTO’23, Davies et al. [25] formally analyzed
L204@P2: WhatsApp’s backup protocol and proposed a passwordprotected key retrieval (PPKR) functionality in the UC
L205@P2: framework. Our M3PM functionalities share similarities
L206@P2: with the PPKR functionality, but there are three main differences: (1) The PPKR functionality employs one password
L207@P2: to retrieve one key, whereas the M3PM functionality utilizes
L208@P2: one master password mpw to retrieve multiple passwords.
L209@P2: This distinction is crucial as a secure M3PM protocol
L210@P2: must safeguard one password even if other passwords are
L211@P2: leaked. (2) The M3PM functionality distinguishes explicit
L212@P2: and implicit authentication. (3) The PPKR functionality
L213@P2: allows an adversary to attempt 10 offline guesses, while our
L214@P2: relaxed M3PM functionality does not restrict the guessing
L215@P2: numbers, which is attributed to the methods in Sec. 6.1.
L216@P2: 3. M3PM Protocols Collection
L217@P2: To address RQ1: What M3PM protocols have been
L218@P2: adopted by existing password managers? we identify the
L219@P2: diverse M3PM protocols in use. In this section, we elaborate
L220@P2: on the process by which we select 43 PMs and collect
L221@P2: information regarding the M3PM for each PM.
L222@P2: 3.1. PMs Selection
L223@P2: To comprehensively analyze various password management schemes, we exhaustively identify PMs from academic
L224@P2: and industrial sources in September and October 2023.
L225@P2: For industrial PMs, we first collect PMs that are popular
L226@P2: with users. We create core search terms (i.e., “password
L227@P2: manager”, “password vault”, “password management”, and
L228@P2: “password store”) and enter each core search term as a
L229@P2: query into the search box on the Chrome Web Store, Google
L230@P2: Play Store, Firefox Add-ons, Edge Add-ons, and Apple’s
L231@P2: App Store. We keep the top 30 PMs displayed in each
L232@P2: query and remove duplicated PMs. To avoid overlooking
L233@P2: popular PMs, we include those recommended annually
L234@P2: by sites like passwordmanager.com, U.S. News, PCMag,
L235@P2: Cybernews, CNET, Tom’s Guide, Forbes, and Security.org.
L236@P2: Leveraging the aforementioned core search terms, we
L237@P2: utilize Github to select relevant open-source PMs and retain
L238@P2: the PMs with over one thousand stars. We consider PMs
L239@P2: with a substantial number of stars on GitHub, as this metric
L240@P2: indicates a stronger appeal and approval among developers.
L241@P2: Given GitHub’s community-driven nature, the number of
L242@P2: stars reflects the PM’s popularity and credibility within the
L243@P2: developer community. All these above steps resulted in 145
L244@P2: PMs from the industry in total.
L245@P2: For academic PMs, we use the above core search terms
L246@P2: to search in DBLP and Google Scholar, and we are only
L247@P2: concerned about papers creating new M3PM protocols.
L248@P2: Finally, we collect 15 PM schemes published in ICDCS,
L249@P2: SecureComm, AsiaCCS, Computers&Security, ESORICS,
L250@P2: IEEE S&P, SOUPS, WWW, USENIX Sec, IEEE TDSC,
L251@P2: JCST, ACSAC, UbiComp, and NSPW.
L252@P2: In the course of our analysis, we refine the pool of
L253@P2: candidate PMs by excluding those with fewer than 10,000
L254@P2: installations, academic PMs with a primary focus other
L255@P2: than security, and PMs that cannot be set up or launched
L256@P2: (confirmed as vendor-related unavailability by all authors).
L257@P2: This process results in a final selection of 43 PMs for our
L258@P2: in-depth research, and we summarize 43 PMs in Table 1.
L259@P2: 3.2. Collection Methodology
L260@P2: In Fig. 1, we present an overview of our collection
L261@P2: methodology. We gather information from various sources,
L262@P2: including documentation sources, data sources, and application sources. All this information is publicly available, and
L263@P2: we do not employ it for any exploitation of PMs.
L264@P2: Documentation sources. For documentation sources, we
L265@P2: use the names of corresponding PMs as core search terms
L266@P2: in popular search engines, Google and Bing. According to
L267@P2: the results of search engines, we collect every descriptive
L268@P2: documentation of PMs, including industrial whitepapers,
L269@P2: README files of open-source PMs, expert blogs, and other
L270@P2: support documentation on PMs’ official websites.
L271@P2: We first search for the descriptions about security and
L272@P2: encryption on each documentation. Subsequently, we extract
L273@P2: the relevant information about algorithms and protocols
L274@P2: from the collected documentation. For example, Bitwarden
L275@P2: has detailed information about its security architecture1.
L276@P2: This includes specifics on how Bitwarden authenticates users

L362@P3: Data sources. For data sources, we use the web page
L363@P3: version of PMs and install browser extensions on Edge
L364@P3: and Chrome. For each PM, we first create an account (we
L365@P3: delete these accounts after research to avoid unnecessary
L366@P3: burdens for PM servers). Furthermore, we use Burp Suite
L367@P3: to record the HTTPS traffic. Following the account creation,
L368@P3: we proceed with a series of essential operations, including
L369@P3: logging in, opening the vault, adding credentials, changing
L370@P3: credentials, deleting credentials, and logging out. In the
L371@P3: subsequent content, we refer to these operations collectively
L372@P3: as PM operations, considering them fundamental actions for
L373@P3: collecting information on M3PM protocols.
L374@P3: Our collection of plaintext network traffic without TLS
L375@P3: aims to discern the communication patterns associated with
L376@P3: M3PM protocols. We do not emphasize TLS because in
L377@P3: the context of M3PM protocols, the server is assumed
L378@P3: to be malicious, rendering the TLS mechanism between
L379@P3: a client and a malicious server ineffective (see details in
L380@P3: Sec. 4.1). Besides, we record crucial data fields for further
L381@P3: code analysis. For example, we find a data field called
L382@P3: “encrypted username” from network traffic with LastPass,
L383@P3: and then we search for this string in the source code to find
L384@P3: where and how the algorithm encrypts usernames.
L385@P3: Furthermore, we install the desktop version of PMs on
L386@P3: different platforms, such as Windows, Linux, and MacOS,
L387@P3: and search for local storage files. We record the plaintext in
L388@P3: data files, and we also record crucial data fields for further
L389@P3: code analysis. Specifically, Zoho Vault provides an offline
L390@P3: version, so we collect the offline version for further research.
L391@P3: Application sources. For application sources, we conduct
L392@P3: static and dynamic analyses of applications. We gather code
L393@P3: from open source code, extension code, and web page
L394@P3: code on the client side. We use the information collected
L395@P3: from documentation and data sources to form core terms
L396@P3: (e.g., “AES256”, “PBKDF2”), and locate the cryptographic
L397@P3: algorithms in the source code.
L398@P3: For dynamic analysis, we use browser developer tools to
L399@P3: set breakpoints at the locations identified by static analysis.
L400@P3: We then execute the PM operations, recording the precise
L401@P3: algorithms associated with each operation. During dynamic
L402@P3: analysis, we find the exact parameter values for cryptographic algorithms, such as iterations for key derivation
L403@P3: functions. To address the challenges posed by JavaScript
L404@P3: obfuscation and diverse front-end technology stacks, we
L405@P3: conduct iterative dynamic analyses and validate the results
L406@P3: collaboratively among the authors.
L407@P3: 3.3. Collection Results
L408@P3: In this section, we answer RQ1 and give an overview of
L409@P3: our collection results, including M3PM protocols, cryptographic algorithms in protocols, and metadata encryption.
L410@P3: All the results are open [7], and we record as many
L411@P3: details as we can to enhance the reproducibility of our
L412@P3: work. Overall, (1) 24 of 36 industrial password managers
L413@P3: are analyzed using reverse engineering; (2) 32 managers
L414@P3: provide useful information in local data files or network data
L415@P3: packets; (3) Only six managers are primarily analyzed using
L416@P3: documentation. In all, 27 managers collect sufficient information for in-depth analysis. Note that when the data logs
L417@P3: provide sufficient information, we do not perform reverse
L418@P3: engineering. For instance, during our network capture, we
L419@P3: observed that Delinea Web does not encrypt any data, which
L420@P3: eliminates the need for further static or dynamic analysis.

L48: # Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions
L49: 
L50: Jinghan Xu    Longze Fan    Zeyuan Wang    Xinjin Li    Hankai Liu\corresponding
L51: ###### Abstract
L52: Tool-using large language model agents frequently replan, retry failed operations, delegate tasks, and resume after crashes. These behaviors can cause one user authorization to be requested and executed multiple times under freshly issued token identifiers, even when each individual token is single-use. We call this failure semantic replay: exceeding the execution budget of a token-independent authorization instance rather than merely reusing an old token identifier.
L53: We show that identifier-local token consumption cannot prevent fresh reissuance unless the issuer retains monotonic durable state over the authorized action, confirmation event, and remaining execution budget. We introduce CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that follows proposal- and authority-level defenses, binds an authenticated user confirmation to a canonical action, and enforces transactional Issue–Prepare–Commit transitions.
L54: Across LLM-agent replanning, retry, delegation, concurrency, confirmation-replay, and crash-recovery scenarios, identifier-local tokens permit fresh semantic reissuance, whereas CapLease and an equally stateful Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission and, with an idempotent sink, duplicate external effects. Our results identify durable authorization state—not token representation alone—as the systems requirement for replay-resistant agent execution.

L10: As digital identity verification becomes increasingly pervasive, existing privacy-preserving approaches are still limited by complex circuit designs, large proof sizes, trusted setups, or high latency. We present Vega, a practical zero-knowledge proof system that proves statements about existing credentials without revealing anything else.
L11: Vega is simple, does not require a trusted setup, and is more efficient than the prior state-of-the-art: for a 1920-byte credential, Vega achieves 92 ms proving time, 23 ms verification time, 108 kB proofs, and a 464 kB proving key. For smaller credentials (896 bytes), these drop to 62 ms proving, 17 ms verification, and 83 kB proofs. At the heart of Vega are two principles that together enable a lightweight proof system that pays only for what it needs.
L12: First, fold-and-reuse proving exploits repetition and folding opportunities (i) across presentations, by pushing repeated work to a rerandomizable precomputation; (ii) across uniform hashing steps, by folding many steps into a single step; and (iii) for zero-knowledge, by folding the public-coin transcript with a random one.
L13: Second, lookup-centric arithmetization extracts relevant values from credential bytes, both for extracting relevant fields without full in-circuit parsing, and to enable length-hiding hashing.

L29: #### Paper 2022/878
L30: 
L31: ### 【17†zk-creds: Flexible Anonymous Credentials from zkSNARKs and Existing Identity Infrastructure】
L32: 
L33: Michael Rosenberg, University of Maryland
L34: 
L35: Jacob White, Purdue University
L36: 
L37: Christina Garman, Purdue University
L38: 
L39: Ian Miers, University of Maryland
L40: ##### Abstract
L41: Frequently, users on the web need to show that they are, for example, not a robot, old enough to access an age restricted video, or eligible to download an ebook from their local public library without being tracked. Anonymous credentials were developed to address these concerns. However, existing schemes do not handle the realities of deployment or the complexities of real-world identity.
L42: Instead, they implicitly make assumptions such as there being an issuing authority for anonymous credentials that, for real applications, requires the local department of motor vehicles to issue sophisticated cryptographic tokens to show users are over 18. In reality, there are multiple trust sources for a given identity attribute, their credentials have distinctively different formats, and many, if not all, issuers are unwilling to adopt new protocols.
L43: We present and build zk-creds, a protocol that uses general-purpose zero-knowledge proofs to 1) remove the need for credential issuers to hold signing keys: credentials can be issued to a bulletin board instantiated as a transparency log, Byzantine system, or even a blockchain; 2) convert existing identity documents into anonymous credentials without modifying documents or coordinating with their issuing authority; 3) allow for flexible, composable, and complex identity statements over multiple credentials.
L44: Concretely, identity assertions using zk-creds take less than 150ms in a real-world scenario of using a passport to anonymously access age-restricted videos.

L31: ### 【17†INDIANA - Verifying (Random) Probing Security through Indistinguishability Analysis】
L32: 
L33: Christof Beierle, Ruhr University Bochum
L34: 
L35: Jakob Feldtkeller, Ruhr University Bochum
L36: 
L37: Anna Guinet, Ruhr University Bochum
L38: 
L39: Tim Güneysu, Ruhr University Bochum, German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence
L40: 
L41: Gregor Leander, Ruhr University Bochum
L42: 
L43: Jan Richter-Brockmann, Ruhr University Bochum
L44: 
L45: Pascal Sasdrich, Ruhr University Bochum
L46: ##### Abstract
L47: While masking is a widely used defense against passive side-channel attacks, its secure implementation in hardware continues to be a manual, complex, and error-prone process. This paper introduces INDIANA, a comprehensive security verification methodology for hardware masking. Our results include a hardware verification tool, enabling a complete analysis of simulation-based security in the glitch-extended probing model and intra-cycle estimations for leakage probabilities in the random probing model.
L48: Notably, INDIANA is the first framework to analyze arbitrary masked circuits in both models, even at the scale of full SPN cipher rounds (e.g., AES), while delivering exact verification results. To achieve accurate and comprehensive verification, we propose a partitionable probing distinguisher that allows for fast validation of probe tuples, surpassing current methods that rely on statistical independence.
L49: Furthermore, our approach naturally supports extensions to the random probing model by utilizing Fast Fourier-Hadamard Transformations (FHTs). Benchmark results show that INDIANA competes effectively with leading probing model verification tools, such as ironMask, maskVerif, and VERICA. INDIANA is also the first tool that is capable to provide intra-cycle estimations of random probing leakage probabilities for large-scalemasked circuits.

[2608.01710] Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01710)
【turn614444view3】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: find({"ref_id":"turn642959view2","pattern":"idempotent"}); Total lines: 159
L16: > Abstract:Tool-using large language model agents frequently replan, retry failed operations, delegate tasks, and resume after crashes. These behaviors can cause one user authorization to be requested and executed multiple times under freshly issued token identifiers, even when each individual token is single-use. We call this failure semantic replay: exceeding the execution budget of a token-independent authorization instance rather than merely reusing an old token identifier.
L17: We show that identifier-local token consumption cannot prevent fresh reissuance unless the issuer retains monotonic durable state over the authorized action, confirmation event, and remaining execution budget. We introduce CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer that follows proposal- and authority-level defenses, binds an authenticated user confirmation to a canonical action, and enforces transactional Issue-Prepare-Commit transitions.
L18: Across LLM-agent replanning, retry, delegation, concurrency, confirmation-replay, and crash-recovery scenarios, identifier-local tokens permit fresh semantic reissuance, whereas CapLease and an equally stateful Server Ledger prevent duplicate admission and, with an idempotent sink, duplicate external effects. Our results identify durable authorization state, rather than token representation alone, as the systems requirement for replay-resistant agent execution.

L925: ### B.3 Security Properties and Limitations
L926: 
L927: The enforcement architecture provides several properties.
L928: 
L929:   * •
L930: 
L931: Authorization on query edges. Unauthorized agent pairs are blocked before the query reaches the target by a deterministic Datalog rule, with no LLM involvement.
L932: 
L933:   * •
L934: 
L935: Source anonymity. The target agent does not know which agent is asking, preventing social engineering from compromised agents.
L936: 
L937:   * •
L938: Memory isolation. Inter-agent exchanges are structurally excluded from all agent memory layers (transcripts, daily logs, search index). The dependency graph is the sole persistence layer for cross-agent traffic, and agents cannot read from it.
L939: 
L940:   * •
L941: 
L942: Retry convergence. On retry, the LLM receives only its rejected response and the denial reason, not the raw retrieval context. It can only subtract information, so the retry loop converges toward policy compliance.
L943: 
L944:   * •
L945: Noninterference. The target agent’s workspace state is invariant to being queried. No transcripts, memory files, or search index entries are created or modified by the inter-agent exchange.
L946: ##### Limitations.
L947: Semantic enforcement via llm_check is inherently probabilistic. A false negative, that is, a failure to detect “doctor appointment” in a cleverly worded response, is a privacy breach. Structural rules are deterministic but cannot express content-level policies. Combining both modes covers a wider policy space, but characterizing llm_check error rates under adversarial conditions remains an open problem.
L948: The Datalog policy rules are hand-authored for this deployment, and generalizing policy authoring to end users is future work.
L949: ## Appendix C Case Study: Coding Agent Security in VS Code Copilot Chat
L950: We demonstrate FORGE applied to a coding agent in VS Code Copilot Chat [【247†41】]. The agent has full access to the workspace through tools that read, edit, and write files, and that run shell commands, including the ability to push commits to remote repositories. While code in the local workspace can be reviewed and rolled back, code pushed to the remote becomes a public artifact flowing through CI and downstream consumers.
L951: A single agent turn can therefore publish vulnerable code or dependencies or a hardcoded API keyalongside any feature it lands. Deterministic gates at the push boundary rather than prompt-level guardrails that do not survive adversarial framing, are required.
L952: ##### Deployment.
L953: 
L954: Copilot is given access to security tools through an MCP service; these include a Gitleaks-based secret scanning tool gitleaks_scan, a dependency scanner based on OSV-Scanner osv_scan, and a SAST scanning tool sast_scan based on Opengrep and Bandit.
L955: The policy specifies three gates that must hold before any git push is allowed. Every edit reaching the push must be transitively followed by a passing gitleaks_scan, every edit to a dependency manifest must be followed by a passing osv_scan, and every edit must be followed by a passing sast_scan. Reachability is defined over the dependency graph using ‘DependsOn‘.
L1030: This rule does not change the safety property at the push boundary, since the push gate of Section 【60†C.1】 already guarantees full coverage. It shifts the scan earlier in the session, surfacing violations close to where they were introduced and facilitating remediation. The rule also illustrates a policy that constrains an action’s authorization on its entire backward slice rather than properties of the action itself.
L1031: ### C.3 Security Properties and Limitations
L1032: 
L1033: The policy provides several properties.
L1034: 
L1035:   * •
L1036: 
L1037: Causal coverage. Coverage is defined by reachability in the dependency graph. Running scanners before making edits does not satisfy the gate. Every edit must be followed by a passing scan that flows into the push.
L1038: 
L1039:   * •
L1040: Scan integrity. Scan results are registered as ToolResult events with the actual scanner output. The policy matches on PASS in the result body rather than the agent’s own judgment, so the agent cannot claim a scan passed when it did not.
L1041: 
L1042:   * •
L1043: 
L1044: No semantic dependence. Every gate in this deployment is structural. Adversarial framing of the edit content cannot affect the system’s judgement of the vulnerability of the generated code.
L1045: ##### Limitations.
L1046: The deployment trusts the security tools it invokes. A false negative in any underlying scanner is a false negative for the policy. The threshold in Section 【61†C.2】 is a heuristic chosen for end-to-end demos and would need tuning for larger projects. The policy rules are authored against the specific tool surface of Copilot Chat, and extending the policy to a different agent host requires enumerating that host’s edit-like and push-like tools, though the underlying coverage logic is unchanged.

L116: To handle context-dependent security requirements, Progent utilizes an LLM to automatically generate the initial policy from the user’s task and updates it as new information arrives during execution. This allows security enforcement to adapt to both task and execution context while minimizing manual effort. However, introducing an LLM for policy construction introduces non-determinism, creating a fundamental tension between automation and deterministic enforcement.
L117: To address this, we further propose that each policy update be checked by a deterministic SMT solver as either a narrowing (applied automatically) or an expansion (requiring explicit approval). This ensures that the agent’s effective action space can only narrow without approval, a property we call monotonic confinement. As a result, even if the LLM is manipulated by adversarial inputs, this deterministic check prevents any silent privilege escalation.
L118: At the same time, it preserves utility by allowing controlled privilege expansion when explicitly authorized.
L119: #### Implementation and Evaluation
L120: 
L121: Since Progent operates at the tool-call level, it can be integrated by inserting a separate module between the agent and its tools. This requires no changes to the agent’s internal architecture, making integration non-intrusive and generalizable across diverse agent frameworks.
L122: We evaluate Progent on AgentDojo (【87†Debenedetti et al., 2024】) and ASB (【91†Zhang et al., 2025】). Progent reduces the attack success rate (ASR) from 39.9% to 1.0% on AgentDojo, and from 70.3% to 3.9% on ASB, while maintaining the agent’s utility in both cases. We further conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze key components of Progent, including model choices and policy update approval configurations.
L123: Finally, we extend AgentDojo into an MCP-based benchmark and connect it to various real-world agent frameworks (e.g., LangChain and OpenAI Agents SDK), where we demonstrate the effectiveness of Progent on protecting both single- and multi-agent systems.

L496: #### Model-Level Prompt Injection Defenses
L497: A parallel line of research focuses on addressing prompt injections at the model level, which can be broken down into two categories. The first category trains and deploys guardrail models to detect injected content (【143†Inan et al., 2023】; 【112†ProtectAI.com, 2024】; 【144†Li et al., 2024a】; 【114†Liu et al., 2025】; 【115†Meta, 2025】). L498: Another key distinction is that Progent provides deterministic security enforcement, which guardrail models cannot. The second category of defenses involves fine-tuning agent LLMs to become more resistant to prompt injections (【145†Chen et al., 2025a】; 【146†Chen et al., 2025b】; 【147†Wallace et al., 2024】; 【148†Chen et al., 2025c】). As shown in 【122†Figure 7】, combining Progent and model-level defenses (【148†Chen et al., 2025c】) can provide stronger protections.
L500: ## 11. Conclusion
L501: We propose Progent, a framework that secures AI agents via privilege control at the tool-call level. Progent introduces a privilege control policy consisting of symbolic rules over tool names and arguments, enforced deterministically with no LLM in the decision loop.
L502: To handle diverse tasks and evolving execution contexts, an LLM automatically generates and updates the policy, while a deterministic SMT-based check determines whether each update is a narrowing (applied automatically) or an expansion (requiring approval), guaranteeing monotonic confinement.
L503: Our evaluation on AgentDojo and ASB demonstrates that Progent significantly reduces attack success rates while preserving high utility, and integration with real-world agent frameworks such as LangChain and OpenAI Agents SDK confirms its practicality as a non-intrusive defense-in-depth layer.

L319: 
L320: An authorized operation is a canonical protocol tuple
L321: 
L322:  | $$o:=(\mathsf{act},\,\mathsf{bind},\,\mathsf{valid}),$$  |
L323: where $\mathsf{act}:=(\mathsf{type},\mathsf{target},\mathsf{scope})$, $\mathsf{bind}:=(\mathsf{redeemer},\mathsf{recipient})$, and $\mathsf{valid}:=(\mathsf{expiry},\mathsf{multiplicity})$.
L324: Here $\mathsf{type}$ specifies the semantic class of the secret-backed action (e.g., $\mathsf{use}$, $\mathsf{export}$, $\mathsf{write}$, $\mathsf{rotate}$, $\mathsf{enroll}$, $\mathsf{revoke}$); $\mathsf{target}$ identifies the protected object; $\mathsf{scope}$ carries canonicalized operation-specific constraints; $\mathsf{redeemer}$ identifies the party entitled to redeem; $\mathsf{recipient}$ identifies the intended recipient of any extracting delivery; $\mathsf{expiry}$ bounds the validity window; and $\mathsf{multiplicity}\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\cup\{\infty\}$ sets the grant’s execution budget: $T$ admits at most $\mathsf{multiplicity}$ Phase III executions under the grant before $\mathsf{expiry}$; $1$ consumes the grant at first redemption (high-authority transaction-style actions), and $\infty$ yields a standing grant ($U$-declared low-risk repeat patterns such as inbox reads).
L325: Freshness for the Phase II verification is enforced separately, via the single-use token $r$ issued at Phase II.1 and consumed at Phase II.3.
L326: We reserve specific terms: a grant $G$ is the protocol artifact representing $U$’s authorization of $o$; it commits to $o$ and conveys for redemption both the authorization signature and the acting credential’s wrapping key (the full structure is in §【41†V-F】). The wrapping key is secret: $G$ is therefore not a public bearer token, and the $U\to T$ leg carrying it requires end-to-end confidentiality. A redeemed grant $\rho$ is $G$’s custodian-internal post-validation form.
L327: SUDP binds $G$ and $\rho$ to the same $\beta$ commitment in Phase II so that the artifact $T$ redeems matches the one $U$ authorized.
L328: SUDP’s cryptographic binding attaches to the canonical bytes of $o$. Two deployment obligations anchor those bytes at the endpoints of the authorization; AV and OB hold when both are met.

L330: 
L331: $\mathsf{Render}(o)$ is deterministic, complete, and confined to $U$’s trusted client, so $U$ approves exactly what $\mathsf{H}(o)$ commits.

L334: 
L335: The action performed at $E$ is a deterministic function of $o$, the material $T$ unwraps, and any auxiliary content that $o$ commits by hash. No authority-relevant input enters between $U$’s authorization and the action.

L377: Ambiguity in the encoding can defeat operation binding without violating collision resistance of $\mathsf{H}$: two semantically distinct descriptors may serialize to the same bytes (so that an adversary substitutes $o^{\prime}\neq o$ with the same $\mathsf{H}$-input), or the same descriptor may serialize differently at $U$ and $T$ (so that $U$ authorizes an operation whose canonical form at $T$ differs from the one $\mathsf{Render}$ presented at authorization time).

L279: ## 4. Formal Model
L280: 
L281: This section defines the object named by a root-scoped quiescence certificate, the evidence required to establish it, and nine results used throughout the paper. Proofs appear in Appendix 【73†A】.
L282: ### 4.1. Root-epoch atoms and machine state
L283: 
L284: Let $\mathcal{R}$ be the set of root identifiers and let $H$ be a collision-resistant digest over an injective, length-delimited canonical encoding. A root-epoch atom is
L285: 
L286:  | $$a=\langle r,e,h_{g}\rangle\in\mathcal{A},$$  |
L287: where $r\in\mathcal{R}$, $e\in\mathbb{N}$ is the root epoch, and $h_{g}$ is the digest of the authenticated grant. Write $\operatorname{rid}(a)=r$ and $\operatorname{rid}(W)=\{\operatorname{rid}(a):a\in W\}$. Root atoms are not bearer strings. An atom is current for a new issuer decision only when the root ledger contains the same grant digest and epoch in phase $\mathsf{ACTIVE}$.
L288: A carrier authorized before retirement can still hold that exact atom while the distributed generation drains; its subsequent effect admission is governed by the relevant provider-local barrier, not by reinterpreting the root cut as an atomic cross-provider fence.
L289: The security-relevant machine state is
L290: 
L291:  | $$S=\langle A,C,X,T,F,K,L,M,P\rangle.$$  |
L292: 
L293: Here $A$ is the root ledger; $C$ the cut ledger; $X$ the carrier registry; $T$ the channel-token ledger; $F$ the endpoint fence map; $K$ the provider commitment/frontier state; $L$ an authenticated event log; $M$ the registered coverage manifests; and $P$ the versioned adapter profiles. Security-changing transitions are serialized within their respective durable domains and use durable idempotency keys.
L294: Let $\preceq_{r}$ be the root ledger’s durable order and, for every endpoint or effect sink $p$, let $\preceq_{p}$ be its durable local admission/log order. Write $\prec_{r}$ and $\prec_{p}$ for their strict parts. The global causal relation $\prec$ is the transitive closure of local durable order, authenticated program order, send-before-accept edges, and observation edges from a committed record to a transition that authenticates that record.
L295: Thus events in different durable domains are compared only through $\prec$, never by comparing their implementation-specific sequence numbers. We use $\nu_{d}(o)$ solely as the local position of event $o$ within durable domain $d$; in particular, $\nu_{r}$ and $\nu_{p}$ are positions within $\preceq_{r}$ and $\preceq_{p}$.
L296: ###### Definition 0 (Linearized root cut).
L297: 
L298: For a current atom $a_{c}=\langle r,e,h_{g}\rangle$, $\mathsf{BeginShutdown}(r,m)$ commits
L299: 
L300:  | $$c=\langle cid,a_{c},e+1,\nu_{r}(c),h_{m},h_{P},h_{T}\rangle$$  |
L301: at root-ledger position $\nu_{r}(c)$. The same transaction retires epoch $e$ by marking $a_{c}$ retired, advances $A(r)$ to the new epoch $e+1$ in phase $\mathsf{DRAINING}$, and freezes manifest digest $h_{m}=H(m)$, profile digest $h_{P}$, and exact cut-target token-frontier digest $h_{T}=H(T_{c})$. The frontier $T_{c}$ is defined below from authoritative pre-cut $\mathsf{SEND}$ records.
L302: Advancing the counter does not issue a successor grant; a later active atom requires a separately authenticated grant transition. The transaction neither revokes the state of a previously authorized carrier nor installs a barrier in any provider domain.
L303: Let $\mathcal{I}_{r}$ contain the issuer events that issue, delegate, reactivate, or enlarge authority under root $r$. A1 requires every $i\in\mathcal{I}_{r}$ to validate its complete selected witness at its own root-ledger linearization point. By contrast, a protected effect has a registered provider-local commitment-admission event $k$. For $k$ at sink $p$, $\nu_{p}(k)$ is the last mediated local decision after which the effect can proceed without another authorization decision.
L304: A settlement, delivery, or physical consequence following $k$ is part of the same commitment, not a fresh commitment. We write $a\in\operatorname{auth}(k)$ when the exact selected authorization witness recorded for $k$ contains atom $a$.
L305: ### 4.2. Minimal support and selected authorization
L306: 
L307: A carrier may have conjunctive requirements and alternative roots. Treating its roots as a flat union would over-revoke independently authorized work; treating them as an existential set would permit root laundering.
L308: ###### Definition 0 (Support antichain).
L309: 
L310: For carrier $x$ in state $S$, its support antichain is a finite family
L311: 
L312:  | $$\Sigma_{S}(x)\subseteq 2^{\mathcal{A}}$$  |
L313: such that every $W\in\Sigma_{S}(x)$ is a sufficient conjunctive authorization witness and no distinct $W,W^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{S}(x)$ satisfies $W\subset W^{\prime}$. The antichain contains all policy-relevant minimal witnesses admitted by the registered derivation profile. The durable field $\operatorname{sel}_{S}(x)\in\Sigma_{S}(x)$ records the witness actually selected for the carrier’s current authority.
L314: Let $\operatorname{Current}_{S}(x,W)$ hold when every atom in $W$ is current and the authenticated derivation edges joining those atoms to $x$ remain valid. A selected witness is an authorization fact, not a planner hint. New issuer decisions require $\operatorname{Current}_{S}(x,\operatorname{sel}_{S}(x))$; effect admission by an already authorized carrier instead presents the exact selected witness to the sink’s barrier rule.

L105: #### Single-use grants and transactional execution.
L106: SUDP binds a fresh single-use grant to a canonical secret-backed operation (【45†Yu et al. 2026】). CapLease shares its exact-action and bounded-use goals but addresses durable state across issuance, admission, and recovery, including reissuance, concurrency, confirmation reuse, and crash duplication.
L107: RPC, secure RPC, transactions, linearizability, and leases provide the underlying mechanisms for uncertain outcomes, principal authentication, atomic updates, and bounded validity (【60†Birrell and Nelson 1984】; 【61†Birrell 1985】; 【62†Gray 1981】; 【63†Herlihy and Wing 1990】; 【64†Gray and Cheriton 1989】). CapLease applies these primitives to token-independent authorization identities and execution budgets at the LLM-agent tool boundary.
L108: ## Problem Formulation and Semantic Replay
L109: #### Agent execution model.
L110: A tool-using agent receives a user task, processes observations and tool outputs, and proposes a call $c=(\mathsf{tool},\mathsf{args})$. Before execution, an upstream authority mechanism evaluates $c$ against trusted context $\gamma$, including the user task, provenance, principal identities, resource scope, and organization policy. If the call is approved, the runtime issues an authorization for use at the protected tool boundary.
L111: We focus on policy-designated high-risk actions with external side effects, such as payments, message transmission, credential changes, and persistent data modification.
L112: #### Authorization identity.
L113: 
L114: A token identifier represents an authorization but does not define its security-relevant identity. We define the token-independent action identity as
L115: 
L116:  | $$\sigma(c,\gamma)=(P_{u},h_{c},h_{a},R),$$  |  | (1)
L117: where $P_{u}$ is the user principal, $h_{c}$ and $h_{a}$ bind the canonical operation and complete arguments, and $R$ identifies the target resource. Tool-specific canonicalization must map effect-equivalent calls to the same identity while separating security-relevant differences. Ambiguous calls are rejected rather than assigned an uncertain authorization identity.
L118: 
L119: We separately define the execution context as
L120: 
L121:  | $$\chi=(P_{e},S,T,v_{p},v_{s}),$$  |  | (2)
L122: where $P_{e}$ is the executor, $S$ and $T$ identify the session and task, and $v_{p},v_{s}$ are the policy and schema epochs. These fields restrict where and by whom an authorization may be used, but do not create a new user-authorized effect.
L123: 
L124: Let $e_{u}$ be an authenticated confirmation event bound to the displayed action, principal, and budget $b$. The authorization instance is

L126:  | $$\alpha=(\sigma,e_{u},b).$$  |  | (3)
L127: A token $z_{i}$ is only one issuance-specific representation of $\alpha$. Consuming $z_{1}$ therefore does not prevent a fresh $z_{2}$ for the same $\alpha$ unless the issuer maintains token-independent state.
L128: #### Threat and trust model.
L129: The adversary may control external content observed by the agent and induce repeated requests through replanning, delegation, concurrent workers, ambiguous tool responses, or lost acknowledgements. It may also copy authorization objects, replay confirmation events, race issuance or admission requests, and attempt cross-principal use. Benign retries and duplicate delivery are also in scope because semantic replay does not require malicious model behavior.
L130: Similar ambiguity arises in remote execution when a caller cannot determine whether a timed-out operation took effect (【60†Birrell and Nelson 1984】).
L131: The adversary cannot forge authenticated principals, confirmation events, provenance records, policy epochs, tool contracts, or committed ledger transitions. Trusted components provide durable atomic storage, authenticated action schemas, semantic canonicalization, and stable confirmation identifiers. Retries of the same confirmation challenge must return the same $e_{u}$.
L132: Incorrect trusted metadata, confirmation duplication, and ledger rollback are trusted-computing-base failures and are evaluated separately.
L133: #### Semantic replay.
L134: 
L135: We define semantic replay as issuing, admitting, or materializing an authorization beyond its budget. Unlike token replay, it may involve fresh identifiers and execution requests. Table 【65†1】 summarizes the considered failures.
L136: Failure  | Description
L137: --- | ---
L138: Old-token replay  | A consumed token is presented again.
L139: Fresh reissuance  | A fresh token represents the same authorization.
L140: Concurrent issuance  | Multiple records are created for the same $(\sigma,e_{u})$.
L141: Concurrent admission  | Multiple executors pass a non-atomic check.
L142: Cross-principal use  | Another executor uses a principal-bound authorization.
L143: Confirmation replay  | One confirmation authorizes multiple instances or budgets.
L144: Crash duplication  | An uncertain outcome triggers a repeated effect.

L705: ### 6.4 Model-Level and Architecture-Level Defenses
L706: Model-level defenses against agent misaligned behavior fall into several categories that attempt to robustify the LLM agent directly. TrustAgent [【152†30】] and Policy-as-Prompt [【151†35】] place policy specifications in prompts, but enforcement is best-effort, and this approach cannot guarantee that the model will necessarily adhere to the policy.
L707: Indirect prompt injection attacks, including those studied by Greshake et al. [【145†28】] and the InjecAgent benchmark [【200†66】], exploit the architectural mixing of instructions and data and can induce agents to violate policies that were specified correctly. Such attacks are considered the most significant risk of using LLM applications [【201†46】], and have motivated various defense mechanisms that have recently been put forth.
L708: For example, detection-based defenses such as Llama Guard [【202†31】] and DataSentinel [【203†39】], as well as training-time defenses such as StruQ [【204†12】], the Instruction Hierarchy [【205†60】], and SecAlign [【206†13】] can be bypassed by adaptive attackers [【207†32】, 【208†43】, 【209†16】]. Architecture-level defenses provide agentic systems designed to bound the effectiveness of prompt injections.
L709: These include CaMeL [【210†20】], which separates control and data flow via a plan-then-execute process, FIDES [【173†18】], which integrates information-flow enforcement into a planner with selective hiding and revealing of tool results, and IsolateGPT [【211†62】], which routes information flow across services through a central hub.
L710: These defenses harden the agent’s reasoning or restrict its architecture, while FORGE mediates at the action boundary and provides deterministic enforcement independent of the agentic system’s architecture or the underlying model behavior.
L711: ### 6.5 Runtime Policy Enforcement for Agents
L712: A growing body of work provides explicit policy languages and runtime enforcement for LLM agents. Progent [【195†56】], NeMo Guardrails [【196†44】], Invariant Guardrails [【164†37】], and AgentSpec [【197†61】] support per-call privilege control, conversational guardrails, and constraints over traces.
L713: ShieldAgent [【198†14】] derives logical rules from policy documents evaluated against deterministic and LLM-backed predicates on the agent’s linear history, while GuardAgent [【199†63】] uses a separate guard LLM to evaluate actions.
L714: Similar to these systems, FORGE also focuses on enforcement at the action boundary. However, FORGE differs from these competing approaches in policy expressiveness, dependency tracking, multi-agent support, and deterministic enforcement. To our knowledge, FORGE is the first to combine all five properties in a single design. Furthermore, FORGE’s formal language applies to more expressive policies compared to prior runtime guardrails.
L715: Specifically, FORGE allows the user to express policies with recursive relations, including transitive closure over the provenance of events. Finally, as far as we are aware, FORGE is the first framework to provide runtime verification for multi-agent systems, where policy decisions can be affected by dependencies that cross agent boundaries. Table 【212†5】 summarizes this.
L716: ## 7 Discussion
L717: ### 7.1 Limitations
L718: Behaviors outside the instrumentation layer. FORGE mediates only actions that pass through instrumented join points. Behaviors that bypass both the framework’s tool-dispatch layer and the instrumented HTTP libraries, such as raw socket writes or direct stdio I/O from agent code, fall outside its mediation boundary. Extending coverage to another channel requires instrumenting the method or library through which that channel is accessed; FORGE makes no guarantees about uninstrumented behavior.
L719: Pre-specified policy intent. FORGE does not infer a security policy dynamically from each open-ended task request. It instead requires an explicit policy to be fixed before execution, and its enforcement guarantee is stated relative to that policy. In contrast, systems such as Conseca [【213†59】] use a language model to synthesize a task-specific policy at runtime.
L720: Although the resulting policy can be enforced deterministically, there is no formal guarantee that the synthesized constraints faithfully represent the user’s intended security requirements. FORGE therefore sacrifices automatic adaptation to previously unseen tasks in order to keep policy synthesis outside its trusted enforcement path. Verified synthesis of task-specific policies remains an open problem.
L721: Intra-method concurrency. The synchronization protocol between the observability service and policy engine assumes that the observability layer executes atomically: the events an instrumented method produces must be registered before any of them can be consumed. This assumption may not hold when an advised method internally launches concurrent tasks that emit messages and no lower-level join point covers those emissions.
L722: In such cases, an authorization query issued during that method’s execution may be evaluated against an incomplete event graph and miss events or dependencies relevant to the decision.
L723: ### 7.2 Future Extensions
L724: 
L725: Incremental policy evaluation. Within a session, the event graph is constructed additively, and is amenable to incremental Datalog evaluation, which would improve scalability to long-context tasks. Incremental evaluation incurs additional overhead, however, recent evaluators such as FlowLog [【214†67】] may bring the crossover with Soufflé [【160†34】] within reach for long-horizon sessions.
L726: Policy language extensions. A Datalog policy is a set of rules over boolean facts, with no first-class notion of time or uncertainty. Temporal operators, in the style of metric first-order temporal logic [【215†4】], would make rate limits and time-bounded obligations declarative without manual bookkeeping over timestamps.
L727: Probabilistic extensions would let a policy propagate the uncertainty of classifier-backed or LLM-backed predicates into the decision, rather than collapsing it to a boolean by thresholding.
L728: ## 8 Conclusion
L729: We present FORGE, a runtime enforcement framework for agentic systems. FORGE allows users to express policies and enforce them by tracking execution history and dependencies across agents and their events. Candidate actions are evaluated before they take effect, allowing deterministic enforcement of context-dependent authorization and workflow constraints. We implement FORGE and evaluate it across four case studies and two real-world deployments.

L31: ### 【17†Randomness Optimization for Gadget Compositions in Higher-Order Masking】
L32: 
L33: Jakob Feldtkeller, Ruhr University Bochum
L34: 
L35: David Knichel, Ruhr University Bochum
L36: 
L37: Pascal Sasdrich, Ruhr University Bochum
L38: 
L39: Amir Moradi, University of Cologne
L40: 
L41: Tim Güneysu, Ruhr University Bochum, German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence
L42: ##### Abstract
L43: Physical characteristics of electronic devices, leaking secret and sensitive information to an adversary with physical access, pose a long-known threat to cryptographic hardware implementations. Among a variety of proposed countermeasures against such Side-Channel Analysis attacks, masking has emerged as a promising, but often costly, candidate. Furthermore, the manual realization of masked implementations has proven error-prone and often introduces flaws, possibly resulting in insecure circuits.
L44: In the context of automatic masking, a new line of research emerged, aiming to replace each physical gate with a secure gadget that fulfills well-defined properties, guaranteeing security when interconnected to a large circuit. Unfortunately, those gadgets introduce a significant amount of additional overhead into the design, in terms of area, latency, and randomness requirements.
L45: In this work, we present a novel approach to reduce the demands for randomness in such gadget-composed circuits by reusing randomness across gadgets while maintaining security in the probing adversary model. To this end, we embedded the corresponding optimization passes into an Electronic Design Automation toolchain, able to construct, optimize, and implement masked circuits, starting from an unprotected design.
L46: As such, our security-aware optimization offers an additional building block for existing or new Electronic Design Automation frameworks, where security is considered a first-class design constraint

L31: ### 【17†LegoSNARK: Modular Design and Composition of Succinct Zero-Knowledge Proofs】
L32: 
L33: Matteo Campanelli, IMDEA Software Institute
L34: 
L35: Dario Fiore, IMDEA Software Institute
L36: 
L37: Anaïs Querol, IMDEA Software Institute, Universidad Politécnica de Madrid
L38: ##### Abstract
L39: We study the problem of building SNARKs modularly by linking small specialized “proof gadgets" SNARKs in a lightweight manner. Our motivation is both theoretical and practical. On the theoretical side, modular SNARK designs would be flexible and reusable. In practice, specialized SNARKs have the potential to be more efficient than general-purpose schemes, on which most existing works have focused. If a computation naturally presents different “components" (e.g.
L40: one arithmetic circuit and one boolean circuit), a general-purpose scheme would homogenize them to a single representation with a subsequent cost in performance. Through a modular approach one could instead exploit the nuances of a computation and choose the best gadget for each component.
L41: Our contribution is LegoSNARK, a "toolbox" (or framework) for commit-and-prove zkSNARKs (CP-SNARKs) that includes: 1) General composition tools: build new CP-SNARKs from proof gadgets for basic relations $\mathit{simply}$. 2) A "lifting" tool: add commit-and-prove capabilities to a broad class of existing zkSNARKs $\mathit{efficiently}$. This makes them interoperable (linkable) within the same computation.
L42: For example, one QAP-based scheme can be used prove one component; another GKR-based scheme can be used to prove another. 3) A collection of succinct proof gadgets for a variety of relations. Additionally, through our framework and gadgets, we are able to obtain new succinct proof systems. Notably: – $\mathsf{LegoGro16}$, a commit-and-prove version of Groth16 zkSNARK, that operates over data committed with a classical Pedersen vector commitment, and that achieves a 5000$\times$ speed in proving time.

L31: ### 【17†Full Proof Cryptography: Verifiable Compilation of Efficient Zero-Knowledge Protocols】
L32: 
L33: José Bacelar Almeida, Manuel Barbosa, Endre Bangerter, Gilles Barthe, Stephan Krenn, and Santiago Zanella Béguelin
L34: ##### Abstract
L35: Developers building cryptography into security-sensitive applications face a daunting task. Not only must they understand the security guarantees delivered by the constructions they choose, they must also implement and combine them correctly and efficiently. Cryptographic compilers free developers from having to implement cryptography on their own by turning high-level specifications of security goals into efficient implementations.
L36: Yet, trusting such tools is risky as they rely on complex mathematical machinery and claim security properties that are subtle and difficult to verify. In this paper, we present ZKCrypt, an optimizing cryptographic compiler that achieves an unprecedented level of assurance without sacrificing practicality for a comprehensive class of cryptographic protocols, known as Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Knowledge.
L37: The pipeline of ZKCrypt tightly integrates purpose-built verified compilers and verifying compilers producing formal proofs in the CertiCrypt framework. By combining the guarantees delivered by each stage in the pipeline, ZKCrypt provides assurance that the implementation it outputs securely realizes the high-level proof goal given as input.
L38: We report on the main characteristics of ZKCrypt, highlight new definitions and concepts at its foundations, and illustrate its applicability through a representative example of an anonymous credential system.
L39: Note: Added material on latest developments in the compiler.
